C01.why: Better than typical anomaly horror thanks to a randomized anomaly deck, roles and weekly mutations, but anomaly recognition is memorization: once a player has seen most of the 120 anomalies, nights become a rote checklist and fear drops off sharply. Retention depends on a steady stream of new chapters, which is costly for a small team.
C01.fix: Make anomalies systemic rather than authored: combine modifiers (target x behavior x timing) so new combinations appear without new art. Add an endless 'Night Shift' mode with rising difficulty, a score, and per-run modifiers you pick (risk for reward).

C02.why: The Keep Talking formula works well for repeat play with a fixed friend group, and procedural modules plus role rotation add variety. However, once the rule pages are mastered the challenge collapses, and emote-only play with matchmade strangers is frustrating, so most solo players will drop off.
C02.fix: Rotate the rulebook each season and add rule-mutating modifiers so mastery has to be relearned. Add a ranked 'expert' tier with time pressure and multi-device chains so long-term skill keeps paying off.

C03.why: One-button shared steering is a strong first-session laugh, but the coordination puzzle has a shallow skill ceiling and the novelty fades within a few sessions (Fart Together/Chained Together-style viral spikes, weak tails). Medals and ghosts help a bit; hand-built courses are a content treadmill.
C03.fix: Build modular procedural rivers plus a team race ladder, and give vehicles real upgrade trees with tradeoffs (more thrusters = more chaos) so a crew has something to optimize across sessions.

C04.why: Shop progression and a museum collection give longer-term goals, and Forger Night PvP adds replayable social deduction. However, the detective core is learnable: once players know the tells, inspection becomes a solved checklist (the Papers, Please problem).
C04.fix: Make forgers adapt, with new forgery techniques each week and a forger skill tier that learns from what players catch most. Make Forger Night the main mode, with ranked roles.

C05.why: Asymmetric 1vN with emergent physics and player-invented hiding spots produces different stories every round (Flee the Facility/Murder Mystery-style replay). Role swaps and snitching add social tension. The risks are a shallow ceiling for the Parent role and new houses being expensive to make.
C05.fix: Add a persistent Parent mastery/perk track and kid 'party trick' loadouts so both sides develop skill. Randomize mess and prop layouts per round so house knowledge isn't the whole game.

C06.why: A weekly haystack reset and shared server progress create an appointment hook, but the core is a standard incremental in a falling genre. Finding a needle is luck-dominated, there is little skill to develop, and most players will find it numbers-only after a few days.
C06.fix: Add a meaningful prestige layer with machine synergies and layout puzzles (optimizing a factory), and weekly haystack modifiers that change which builds are optimal.

C07.why: Daily seeded mountains and rope-physics chaos make good repeated friend sessions, but Chained Together-style games are 'beat it once' experiences and on Roblox this space is flooded. Procedural mountains that stay fun to climb are hard to generate well.
C07.fix: Add run modifiers and biome mutators, a permanent mountaineering skill/gear progression, and a weekly 'hard peak' with team leaderboard times so crews keep a reason to return.

C08.why: The views-to-gear-to-bigger-channel loop plus procedural layouts and a ghost catalogue give real progression, and the montage payoff is social. However, Content Warning showed a huge launch with a steep falloff, and once the ghost roster is known, scares and footage get repetitive.
C08.fix: Give ghosts behavior combinations and per-run modifiers, plus 'sponsor contracts' (specific shots required) that rotate daily, so each run has a new target rather than 'film anything scary'.

C09.why: Gesture accuracy is a real skill to develop and cross-player spell combos add discovery, but fixed wave defence goes stale once the combo set is known, and drawing on mobile can be fatiguing. Rune-book progression gives medium-term goals.
C09.fix: Turn waves into a roguelite with random rune drafts and relics per run, endless mode leaderboards, and weekly enemy mutators so each 10-minute session plays differently.

C10.why: The strongest structural replay engine here: roguelite runs give per-session variety, and breeding/inheritance builds a unique family tree with mutation chasing (a long-term goal that is both pet-sim collecting and strategy). New traits and mutations are cheap data-driven content, so a small team can keep feeding it.
C10.fix: Add asynchronous PvP or ranked 'bloodline' ladders and seasonal mutation pools so endgame lineages have a competitive outlet beyond collecting.

C11.why: The extraction risk/reward loop (greed vs survival) is proven for repeat play (R.E.P.O., Lethal Company), and procedural rooms plus gear tiers support many runs. The entity can become predictable and liminal visuals lose their eeriness with repeat exposure.
C11.fix: Add several entity types with distinct rules drawn per contract, plus contract modifiers and a quota system across multi-run 'shifts' that pressures risk-taking.

C12.why: Role-split emergencies are fun the first several times, but the pitch is thin on depth: emergencies are a finite set, and once the crew learns the responses it turns into a procedure. Aircraft unlocks are mostly reskins of the same coordination.
C12.fix: Build stacking, cascading failures (one fix causes another) and a campaign of escalating routes with permadeath crew careers and ranks so there is long-term mastery and stakes.

C13.why: Mass-player strategy produces emergent, never-repeating matches driven by diplomacy and betrayal, with a high skill ceiling and a season ladder. OpenFront-style games retain their core players well, and content is cheap (new maps). Risks: snowballing stomps for new players and needing 50 players to start a match.
C13.fix: Add skill-based lobby tiers or a beginner continent, plus short 'comeback' mechanics or vassal play for eliminated players so losers re-queue instead of quitting.

C14.why: The physics-comedy delivery loop is fun, but it is Overcooked-style level content that a team has to hand-build, and the core action (carry carefully) has limited depth. Courier rank and van upgrades are typical tycoon progression.
C14.fix: Make routes and parcel combinations procedural with daily order boards and rated multi-stop shifts, and treat versus courier mode as a ranked mode with sabotage.

C15.why: The auto-battler format is among the most replayable structures in games (TFT, Merge Tactics): every draft differs, skill compounds, ranked gives long-term goals, and 8-minute matches suit mobile. New toys and synergy sets are cheap, data-driven seasonal content.
C15.fix: Add rotating seasonal sets with new synergies plus a co-op/duos mode and a weekly 'chaos rule' mode to keep it fresh and social for kids who bounce off ranked.

C16.why: Timed chores plus chaos events repeat the same chores with slight variation; there is no skill ceiling or strong long-term goal, and 7 Days Cat-Sitting already owns the anomaly version. Likely played a few times and dropped.
C16.fix: Add a collection-driven meta (adopt and raise your own pets from jobs, pet personalities that combine into random chaos) and a co-op rating ladder so shifts have stakes.

C17.why: Tricky Towers proves stacking has a skill ceiling, but the Roblox-friendly co-op version is thin: random pieces and events give some variety, yet sessions feel the same quickly and there are few long-term goals beyond ranked.
C17.fix: Add Tricky Towers-style spell/sabotage items in versus, a puzzle campaign with daily seeded towers, and team ranked with seasons.

C18.why: The weekly battle is a built-in appointment hook for D2–7/D8–28, and shared ownership is novel. However, individual agency per session is low, the daily loop (gather and vote) is a chore, and Roblox servers are ephemeral, which undermines persistence and players' attachment to a server.
C18.fix: Make it 'your monster across servers': a persistent guild/clan monster with daily mini-raids that feed it, and let players control a limb or ability in the battle so the payoff is playable.

C19.why: Hide-in-plain-sight is socially replayable and role swaps keep it fresh for a while, but Be NPC or Die/DISGUISE show the format saturates. Guard play tends to be solved by watching for anyone not moving like an NPC.
C19.fix: Add statue abilities and guard gadget loadouts with progression, random museum layouts and NPC behavior sets per round, and a ranked mode.

C20.why: Competitive sports with ranked is inherently replayable (Volleyball Legends retains well), but one-touch tap controls lower the skill ceiling, which is the main replay driver, and the content is thin against an entrenched incumbent.
C20.fix: Add mastery depth (spike timing, feints, positional abilities), a 2v2 ranked season ladder, and team/club progression.

overall_notes: Replay leaders are systemic, skill-compounding or PvP-emergent designs whose content is cheap data: C15 auto-battler, C10 roguelite and breeding, C13 mass strategy, then C05 and C11. Most co-op novelty concepts (C03, C07, C12, C14, C16, C17) are first-session laugh machines with weak tails, the Squad Busters/Fart Together risk. Anomaly and detective concepts (C01, C04) have a memorization ceiling and need systemic or adaptive content to escape 'finished once played'. Common fix pattern: add a roguelite/modifier layer per run, a long-term ranked or collection meta, and data-driven seasonal content rather than hand-built levels.
